summary:
BLINKx is a free web tool that turns NASA SPHEREx infrared images into a flipbook you can blink through, so moving and changing objects stand out.
You type any star name or sky coordinates, and it finds every SPHEREx image of that spot in NASA's archive. It reads only the pixels it needs straight from NASA's cloud copy and plays them over time.
Pick any of SPHEREx's six wavelength bands, switch on difference mode to light up what moved, and pin an object twice to measure its speed.
Click a spot to get its spectrum and a light curve, then check your find against Gaia and NASA WISE catalogues.
Arrow tabs let you sweep across nearby sky, and every view is a shareable link.

It answers the "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge directly: coordinates in, animation out, with real data checks.
It measures Barnard's Star moving 10.2″/yr against the catalogue's 10.4″/yr.
It shows WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, appearing only at 4.7 µm exactly where its motion predicts.

Hidden cold worlds are too faint to find in visible light, and spotting them takes many human eyes.
BLINKx gives anyone with a browser the tools to search for them.
details:
What it does and how it works

BLINKx is a web tool for searching NASA SPHEREx infrared images for things that move or change.

You type a star name or RA/Dec, or pick one of five challenge targets.

It then plays every SPHEREx image of that patch of sky as a flipbook.

1. Find the images. The app searches NASA/IPAC IRSA for every SPHEREx Level 2 image covering the position, including newly released data. Star names are looked up in SIMBAD.

2. Cut out only what's needed. It reads just the needed pixels from NASA's public S3 copy of the archive using HTTP Range requests, so it never downloads whole files. Then it turns each image north-up so frames taken at different spacecraft angles line up.

3. Group and blink. Frames are stacked per 6-month survey pass, per day, or shown one by one, in any mix of SPHEREx's six detector bands (0.75-5 µm).

4. Analyse.

- Difference mode subtracts a reference frame, so anything that moved shows as an orange/blue pair.

- You can pin an object in two frames to measure its proper motion.

- Clicking any spot gives its spectrum and brightness over time.

- Pipeline quality flags are read for each image, and flagged exposures can be skipped.

5. Check your find. Gaia DR3 stars (moved to each frame's date) and NASA WISE (CatWISE2020) sources can be overlaid. Objects WISE measured moving show their speed.

6. Explore. Arrow tabs step the view across neighbouring sky, and the next patches load in the background.

Benefits

- Nothing to install and no FITS files to handle. It runs in any browser, and every view is a shareable URL.

- Checked on real data.

- Barnard's Star: 10.2″/yr measured, against 10.4″/yr in the catalogue.

- WISE 0855: appears only at 4.7 µm, exactly where its motion predicts. WISE's own catalogue gives 8.1″/yr for the same object.

- Epsilon Indi B: 458 exposures make a spectrum showing a T dwarf's methane absorption.

- Works with new data automatically, because each search goes to the live archive.

Intended impact

Cold brown dwarfs and possible distant planets are almost invisible in visible light, and finding them takes many eyes.

Projects like Backyard Worlds showed that volunteers can find them by blinking images.

BLINKx brings that method to SPHd data, so students, amateurs and researchers can search with the same tools.

Tools and technologies

- Language: TypeScript throughout.

- Frontend: React, Vite, TailwinHTML Canvas and SVG for imagesand charts.

- API: Express, running as a Ver the same AWS region as NASA'sdata, so frames are cut close to where they're stored.

- SPHEREx code written from scratch: a FITS header parser, the TAN-SIP sky-coordinate maths, a RICE decompressor for the quality-flag data, and wavelength lookup.

- Data services: IRSA SIA and GaA Gaia, CatWISE2020 and SIMBAD.

- Storage: Supabase, for search caching and the pre-cut demo targets.

Creativity

- Wavelength as a discovery tool: you can watch WISE 0855 appear when you switch from 0.9

to 4.7 µm.

- A spectrum from a flipbook: SPHEREx's filters mean each exposure samples a slightly

different wavelength, so all octrum.

- A second telescope as a cross-check: WISE results are shown next to the SPHEREx images.

- Explore mode: turns looking ate nearby sky.

Factors we considered

- Accuracy:

- Every frame shows its date, band and exposure count.

- The WISE overlay filters outt stars.

- Claims were softened wherever saturation affects the data.

- Speed and reliability:

- Archive calls are retried, because IRSA intermittently returns 502 errors.

- Archive searches are cached,cut, and nearby frame lists arereused when exploring.

- Ease of use: an (i) help popovd layouts tested at laptop andphone sizes.

- Openness: data credits are shoshared as a link.
